site.name: the Motion Social Club
site.title: the Motion Social Club
site.description: The side companion on your motion design path. A place to connect with other people, to practice, and to embrace failure.
site.positioning: tMSC was born out of the need to find valuable resources and foster meaningful discussions that go beyond the technical aspects of motion design.

pillars.name: Structure
pillars.text: Helping someone find their way in — curated paths, resources, and exercises that make the first steps in motion design less lonely.

pillars.name: Criticism
pillars.text: Looking at real work and saying why it works or doesn't. Building the human criteria that no tool can replace.

pillars.name: Honesty
pillars.text: Naming the human experience of the work — the doubts, the mistakes, the real life around the practice.

threads.name: Practice over tutorials
threads.text: Watching is not the same as learning. Short, bounded exercises beat one more tutorial every time.

threads.name: Fundamentals over tools
threads.text: Easing, timing, contrast, hierarchy. Tools are exhausting — foundations are permanent.

threads.name: Small and consistent
threads.text: The gym metaphor: short sessions, no pressure for perfection. The work no one sees shapes your skill.

threads.name: Community and real connection
threads.text: Real conversations over algorithm-driven encounters. Motion design shouldn't feel this lonely.

threads.name: Transparency
threads.text: Uncertainty, mistakes, and real life are part of the voice — not something to edit out.

practiceFiles.name: Contrast
practiceFiles.note: Start here — black and white only

practiceStages.name: Before the software
practiceStages.goal: Decisions before tools. You sketch how something moves, then make exactly one thing move.

practiceStages.name: The first month
practiceStages.goal: The fundamentals that make motion feel intentional: curves, hierarchy, timing, type.

practiceStages.name: Make it interactive
practiceStages.goal: Stop thinking in timelines. Start thinking in states, conditions and the person clicking.

practiceStages.name: Ship something
practiceStages.goal: Finish small pieces, keep them consistent, and get them out of the folder.

practiceExercises.title: What actually excites you
practiceExercises.goal: Decide what you are practicing for, before you practice anything.
practiceExercises.brief:
Write down the design work you already do.
Write down the motion work you would be excited to show someone.
Circle the overlap. That is your first project.
practiceExercises.constraint: Don't research. Don't open a single reference. Fifteen minutes, your own head.
practiceExercises.done: Three sentences on paper you can come back to every time you get stuck.

practiceExercises.title: Sketch how it moves
practiceExercises.goal: Think in motion before a timeline can talk you out of it.
practiceExercises.brief:
Pick a poster, a logo or a screen you already designed.
Write three to five words for the feeling it should have.
Draw three frames: beginning, middle, end.
Mark what moves first and what waits.
practiceExercises.constraint: No software. Paper only. We're not looking for the right answer, we're widening what's possible.
practiceExercises.done: Three frames and an order of events.

practiceExercises.title: One element, one move
practiceExercises.goal: Break the gap between watching and doing.
practiceExercises.brief:
Import the design you sketched.
Pick ONE element — the title, one shape, one icon.
Animate it with Position or Scale. Nothing else.
Apply Easy Ease, then open the Graph Editor and drag the handles.
Loop the preview ten times.
practiceExercises.constraint: One element. Two properties, maximum. Resist the second element.
practiceExercises.done: Something moves, and you can say why it moves that way.
practiceExercises.watch: Learn After Effects in 10 Minutes — Ben Marriott

practiceExercises.title: The interface tour
practiceExercises.goal: Know where things are — not how everything works.
practiceExercises.brief:
Watch one intro tutorial. One.
As you watch, make a composition, drop in a shape and set two keyframes.
Stop at sixty minutes even if the video isn't over.
practiceExercises.constraint: One hour, then close the video. Theory without practice doesn't stick.
practiceExercises.done: You can make a comp, import a file and set a keyframe without looking it up.
practiceExercises.watch: I'll Teach You After Effects in 60 Minutes — Ben Marriott

practiceExercises.title: Five minutes of easing
practiceExercises.goal: Feel the difference easing makes, instead of reading about it.
practiceExercises.brief:
Take a square. Move it left to right over one second.
Duplicate it twice.
One linear, one Easy Ease, one with custom curves in the Graph Editor.
Stack them and play all three together.
practiceExercises.constraint: Same distance, same duration, every time. Only the curve changes.
practiceExercises.done: You can name which one feels expensive, and say why.
practiceExercises.watch: The LAST Graph Editor Tutorial You'll Ever Need — Jake In Motion

practiceExercises.title: Three adjectives, three moves
practiceExercises.goal: Connect brand personality to movement before you animate anything.
practiceExercises.brief:
Pick a brand you like. Write three adjectives for it.
For each one, write a sentence describing how its logo would enter the frame.
Be specific: how fast, from where, does it overshoot or settle?
practiceExercises.constraint: Words only. If you can't describe it, you can't animate it.
practiceExercises.done: Three sentences you could hand to another animator.

practiceExercises.title: Steal three beats
practiceExercises.goal: Learn to see timing instead of effects.
practiceExercises.brief:
Find a five-second piece you love.
Watch it five times without pausing.
Write down the three moments where something changes.
Note the gap between them in frames, not in feelings.
practiceExercises.constraint: No recreating. Only watching and counting.
practiceExercises.done: Three timestamps and the rhythm between them.
practiceExercises.watch: How to Keyframe Like a Pro — Alex Grigg

practiceExercises.title: Snappy or smooth, pick one
practiceExercises.goal: Get past Easy Ease and into curves you actually chose.
practiceExercises.brief:
Separate dimensions on your Position property.
Animate one move. Open the Graph Editor.
Make a snappy version: fast out, long settle.
Make a smooth version: even, slow at both ends.
Keep both. Name them.
practiceExercises.constraint: Easy Ease is a starting point, never the answer.
practiceExercises.done: Two versions of one move, and a preference you can defend.
practiceExercises.watch: The MoGraph Secret Weapon: the Graph Editor

practiceExercises.title: Parent it to a null
practiceExercises.goal: Move a group without touching the group.
practiceExercises.brief:
Take three elements you've already animated.
Create a Null Object.
Parent all three to it.
Animate only the null — the whole set should travel together.
Then move one child on its own and watch it keep its own life.
practiceExercises.constraint: Don't touch the children's Position once they're parented.
practiceExercises.done: One controller driving a group, children still free.
practiceExercises.watch: Parenting and Null Objects — Adobe

practiceExercises.title: Reveal with a matte
practiceExercises.goal: Learn the difference between hiding something and revealing it.
practiceExercises.brief:
Take a line of type.
Reveal it with a mask drawn directly on the layer.
Undo. Reveal the same line with a shape layer as an alpha matte.
Animate the shape, not the type.
practiceExercises.constraint: Build it both ways before you decide which one you like.
practiceExercises.done: The same reveal built twice, and an opinion about which is easier to change later.
practiceExercises.watch: Track Matte vs Mask in After Effects

practiceExercises.title: Pre-comp and offset
practiceExercises.goal: Build once, reuse everywhere.
practiceExercises.brief:
Animate one small loop — a dot pulsing, a line drawing on.
Pre-compose it.
Duplicate the pre-comp five times.
Slide each copy a few frames later in the timeline.
Change the original and watch all five update.
practiceExercises.constraint: Edit only the source comp. Never the copies.
practiceExercises.done: A sequence built from one asset you can restyle in one place.
practiceExercises.watch: Understanding Precomps — Adobe

practiceExercises.title: Kerning before keyframes
practiceExercises.goal: Fix the type before you animate the type.
practiceExercises.brief:
Set a headline the way you would for print.
Kern it by hand. Fix the leading.
Align it to the centre of the composition, not by eye.
Only then set your first keyframe.
practiceExercises.constraint: No animating until the still frame would survive on its own.
practiceExercises.done: A frozen frame you'd publish as a poster.

practiceExercises.title: Type that arrives
practiceExercises.goal: Animate text without destroying its readability.
practiceExercises.brief:
Set one line of type, centred and properly kerned.
Add a Text Animator: Position, then a Range Selector.
Stagger the characters so the line assembles instead of sliding.
Adjust the offset until it reads before it finishes.
practiceExercises.constraint: Keep the text editable. No converting to shapes today.
practiceExercises.done: A line you can still retype, arriving with a rhythm.
practiceExercises.watch: Text Animators for Beginners

practiceExercises.title: Three elements, one order
practiceExercises.goal: Motion hierarchy: what moves first tells people where to look.
practiceExercises.brief:
Take a layout with three parts — a headline, an image, a label.
Animate all three arriving.
Build version A: headline first.
Build version B: image first.
Watch both. Notice where your eye goes.
practiceExercises.constraint: Same timing, same easing. Only the order changes.
practiceExercises.done: Two versions, and a clear read on what each one says.

practiceExercises.title: Micro-timing offsets
practiceExercises.goal: Find the two to six frames that make an interface feel alive.
practiceExercises.brief:
Animate an icon, a label and a background panel arriving together.
Now offset them: background first, icon three frames later, label three after that.
Try two frames. Try eight.
Find the one that still reads as a single action.
practiceExercises.constraint: The whole thing stays under 500ms.
practiceExercises.done: One stagger you'd ship.

practiceExercises.title: The verb test
practiceExercises.goal: Make one word do one job.
practiceExercises.brief:
Pick a verb: emphasise, guide, interrupt, welcome.
Animate a single word so it performs that verb.
Show it to someone without telling them the verb.
Ask them what it's doing.
practiceExercises.constraint: One word. One verb. Under two seconds.
practiceExercises.done: Somebody guessed the verb.

practiceExercises.title: The brand's natural ease
practiceExercises.goal: Give a brand one curve and use it everywhere.
practiceExercises.brief:
Pick a brand. Write down its speed: quick and decisive, or slow and considered?
Build one easing curve that matches.
Apply that same curve to three different moves — a fade, a slide, a scale.
Save it as an animation preset.
practiceExercises.constraint: One curve. Every move. If one move needs a different curve, change all of them.
practiceExercises.done: A preset file with the brand's name on it.

practiceExercises.title: Analog pass
practiceExercises.goal: Take the digital sheen off a piece that already works.
practiceExercises.brief:
Take an animation you've finished.
Add an Adjustment Layer over everything.
Apply Posterize Time at 12fps.
Add subtle noise or grain.
Compare it against the original.
practiceExercises.constraint: Don't change a single keyframe. Only the pass on top.
practiceExercises.done: The same piece with a different texture, and a decision about which you prefer.

practiceExercises.title: Sketch the states
practiceExercises.goal: Plan an interaction before you build it.
practiceExercises.brief:
Pick one component: a toggle, a menu icon, a like button.
List every state it can be in.
Draw an arrow between each pair that can actually happen.
Mark which arrows need a user, and which happen on their own.
practiceExercises.constraint: Paper. If the diagram is confusing, the build will be worse.
practiceExercises.done: A state diagram with fewer arrows than you first thought you needed.

practiceExercises.title: Your first state machine
practiceExercises.goal: Stop thinking in timelines. Start thinking in states.
practiceExercises.brief:
Draw a simple shape in Design Mode.
Make two timelines: Idle and Active.
Create a State Machine and wire Entry to Idle.
Add a transition from Idle to Active.
Play it, and watch nothing happen until the condition is met.
practiceExercises.constraint: Two states. No listeners yet.
practiceExercises.done: A graph where you can see why it moves.
practiceExercises.watch: Rive 101 — State Machine Overview

practiceExercises.title: The boolean toggle
practiceExercises.goal: One input, two directions, no extra animation.
practiceExercises.brief:
Add a Boolean input called 'on'.
Transition Idle to Active when on is true.
Transition Active to Idle when on is false.
Toggle it in the preview and watch Rive interpolate both ways.
practiceExercises.constraint: You only animate one direction. Let the machine do the other.
practiceExercises.done: A switch that works both ways, from one timeline.
practiceExercises.watch: Rive State Machine Tutorial

practiceExercises.title: Make it respond
practiceExercises.goal: Hand control to the person using it.
practiceExercises.brief:
Draw an invisible rectangle over your shape — the hitbox.
Add a Listener: Pointer Enter sets 'on' to true.
Add another: Pointer Exit sets it false.
Hover. Then make the hitbox slightly bigger than the shape and hover again.
practiceExercises.constraint: Hover only. Clicks are tomorrow.
practiceExercises.done: Something that reacts to you, not to a playhead.
practiceExercises.watch: Rive 101 — Listeners

practiceExercises.title: Exit time
practiceExercises.goal: Stop animations from cutting each other off.
practiceExercises.brief:
Build a press animation that plays on click.
Leave the transition instant — click twice fast and watch it jump.
Now set Exit Time to 100%.
Click twice fast again.
practiceExercises.constraint: Change one setting. Notice everything it fixes.
practiceExercises.done: A press that always finishes what it started.
practiceExercises.watch: Rive 101 — Transitions

practiceExercises.title: A slider from two poses
practiceExercises.goal: Map a whole range of motion to a single number.
practiceExercises.brief:
Make two timelines: Empty and Full.
Create a Blend State mapped from 0 to 100.
Add a Number input and drag it.
Add a condition that fires a 'done' state when it reaches 100.
practiceExercises.constraint: Only two poses. Rive fills in everything between.
practiceExercises.done: A loading bar you can scrub with a number.
practiceExercises.watch: Controlling Animations with Blend States

practiceExercises.title: The interactive button
practiceExercises.goal: Put states, listeners, transitions and timing into one thing that works.
practiceExercises.brief:
Design a button.
Build Idle, Hover, Pressed and Success timelines.
Wire hover with a boolean, press with a trigger.
Use Exit Time so the press always completes.
Export it and open the .riv on your phone.
practiceExercises.constraint: Four states, no more. Polish the transitions instead of adding states.
practiceExercises.done: A button you'd hand to a developer.
practiceExercises.watch: Animated Buttons in Rive

practiceExercises.title: The week's review
practiceExercises.goal: Close the loop so next week isn't a guess.
practiceExercises.brief:
Open the last thing you made.
Write one sentence on what worked.
Write one sentence on what you avoided.
Pick next week's single focus out of the second sentence.
practiceExercises.constraint: It doesn't matter if you missed the hours you planned. Only that you look.
practiceExercises.done: Next week's focus, written down before this week ends.

practiceExercises.title: Export like it's going somewhere
practiceExercises.goal: Learn the last mile before a client teaches it to you.
practiceExercises.brief:
Take a finished piece.
Export it three ways: an MP4 for social, a transparent MOV or Lottie for the web, and a still frame.
Check the file sizes against each other.
Write one line documenting what moves and how long it takes.
practiceExercises.constraint: Name every file yyyy-mm-dd-name. Start the habit today.
practiceExercises.done: Three files, correctly named, and a note anyone could read.
practiceExercises.watch: BEST Export Settings In After Effects

practiceExercises.title: Five seconds, shipped
practiceExercises.goal: Finish something small instead of starting something big.
practiceExercises.brief:
Build a five to eight second vertical post at 1080×1920.
One hero transition. One line of type. One accent.
Grade it, add grain, export an MP4.
Post it, or send it to one person.
practiceExercises.constraint: Under ten seconds, and out the door today.
practiceExercises.done: A file with today's date in its name, seen by someone who isn't you.
practiceExercises.watch: 2 Modern Instagram Reel Animations — Dope Motions

practiceExercises.title: The logo sting
practiceExercises.goal: Two seconds that say what a brand is like.
practiceExercises.brief:
Take a logo — yours, or one you admire.
Write the three adjectives first.
Build a two-second entrance using Position, Scale and Rotation.
Match the easing to the adjectives: elegant means slow settles, energetic means overshoot.
Render it as a loop.
practiceExercises.constraint: Two seconds. No effects, no plugins — transforms and curves only.
practiceExercises.done: A sting where the movement matches the words you wrote first.
practiceExercises.watch: How Dawn Creative Approaches Brand Animation

practiceExercises.title: A set that belongs together
practiceExercises.goal: Make separate animations feel like one system.
practiceExercises.brief:
Pick three to five icons or graphic elements.
Decide the shared rules first: duration, easing curve, direction of entry.
Animate all of them to those rules.
Play them side by side. Fix whichever one breaks the set.
practiceExercises.constraint: Same curve on every piece. If one needs a different curve, change all of them.
practiceExercises.done: Five animations that look like the same person made them.
practiceExercises.watch: Icon Animation Tutorial

practiceExercises.title: One screen, in motion
practiceExercises.goal: Motion that guides instead of decorating.
practiceExercises.brief:
Take a screen you designed.
Animate the entrance: what appears first, what follows, what never moves.
Add one micro-interaction — a button press or a loading state.
Keep the whole entrance under 800ms.
practiceExercises.constraint: If a movement doesn't tell the user something, delete it.
practiceExercises.done: A screen transition you'd defend in a design review.

practiceExercises.title: Information, one beat at a time
practiceExercises.goal: Reveal data so it's understood, not just decorated.
practiceExercises.brief:
Take three numbers that mean something together.
Storyboard the order they should land in.
Build a ten to fifteen second piece: masks for the bars, text animators for the figures.
Remove anything that moves without earning it.
practiceExercises.constraint: One idea on screen at a time.
practiceExercises.done: Somebody watched it once and could repeat the point.
practiceExercises.watch: Infographics Beginners Tutorial in After Effects

practiceRules: Consistency beats intensity. Thirty minutes you actually do beats a five-hour session you keep postponing.
Set the goal small enough that you can't fail. One element moving is a finished session.
Animate one parameter at a time. Enter is ease out, exit is ease in, emphasis is ease in-out.
Use designs you already have. "What should I animate?" is the question that ends most practices.
Name every file yyyy-mm-dd so a month from now you can see the distance you covered.
It doesn't matter if you set an expectation and didn't fill it up. What matters is that you come back next week.
